title: Krishna the negotiator
hook: five villages; Duryodhana refuses a needle's point of land

segments.voice: Yesterday: thirteen years, twelve in the forest and one hiding in plain sight. Your line was the year of hiding. Were you gentle with someone quiet? Day seventy-five.

Have you ever tried to make peace between two people who both think they're right? You go back and forth. You shrink the ask. You offer the smallest possible thing that might let everyone save face. The thirteen years are over. The Pandavas kept every term of the bet. Now they want their kingdom back. Duryodhana says no. Both sides start gathering armies from every kingdom in the land. And one person tries, one last time, to stop the war. Krishna. Cousin to the Pandavas, friend to Arjuna, and, as many Hindus believe, God himself on earth. He goes to Hastinapura, alone, as an envoy of peace.
screen: `MAKING PEACE BETWEEN TWO SIDES.` → `THE TERMS WERE KEPT.` → `KRISHNA GOES, ALONE, FOR PEACE.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana prepares a feast to win him over. Krishna refuses it and goes instead to eat at the house of Vidura, the king's wise and humble half-brother. A small, telling choice. Then he stands in the great hall, in front of the blind king, the elders, and Duryodhana, and speaks for peace. Give the Pandavas their half of the kingdom, he says. And when that's refused, he makes the smallest ask the story knows. Give them five villages. Just five. One for each brother. They'll accept that and there will be no war. Think about that offer. Kings who once ruled a shining city, after thirteen years of exile, asking for five villages. And Duryodhana's answer has become a proverb across India. In the story, he says he won't give them even as much land as can be pierced by the point of a needle. Not without a war. His own parents beg him. The elders beg him. He walks out of the hall. He even plots to seize Krishna. And in the tradition, Krishna reveals himself in that moment, showing the court a vast, blazing form filled with gods and worlds, so bright that only a few can look. Then he leaves. The war is coming. Here's what the story knows. Wars rarely start over something big. They start when someone refuses something small. Five villages would have saved millions, in the story's numbers. A needle's point of land was too much to give. Most family fights, most feuds, have a five-villages moment: a small, fair ask that one side just won't grant.
screen: `THE FEAST REFUSED; VIDURA'S TABLE.` · `HALF THE KINGDOM. THEN FIVE VILLAGES.` · `NOT A NEEDLE'S POINT OF LAND.` · `WARS START WHEN THE SMALL ASK IS REFUSED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly. Think of a conflict in your life, big or small, that's stuck. Now look for its five villages: the smallest fair thing that could let it move. An apology. One phone call. Giving back one thing. Letting someone else be right about one point. Maybe it's something you could offer. Maybe it's something you've been refusing. Don't decide anything yet. Just find the five villages, and hold them. The bell holds the time.
Krishna the negotiator. The envoy who asked for half a kingdom, then five villages, and got not even a needle's point.
Your line: five villages. Today, in one argument, make the smallest fair offer you can, or accept one someone makes to you. Day seventy-five.

howItsDone: Krishna's peace mission, the Udyoga Parva's embassy, is told in Mahabharata recitations and dance dramas such as Kathakali, and 'not a needle's point of land' is a saying many Indians use for stubborn refusal.

fork.setup: you're Krishna. Duryodhana has refused to return half the kingdom. war is days away. what do you ask for?
options: walk out and prepare for war.
fork.reveal: he asks for five villages, one for each brother. Duryodhana refuses even a needle's point of land, and the war becomes certain.

original.note: Sanskrit: suchi (needle) + agra (point). The needle's point of land Duryodhana wouldn't give.

trapdoor: what you thought: the great war was about a whole kingdom.
what it means: it came down to five villages, and a man who wouldn't give a needle's point of land.
what a scholar hears: Krishna's embassy is in the Udyoga Parva; tradition places his cosmic form in the Kaurava court, a first glimpse before the Gita.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Krishna's embassy; Vidura's house; the five villages; Duryodhana's refusal; the cosmic form in the court)

notes: The five-villages request: in the Udyoga Parva it is Yudhishthira's offer, which Krishna carries; the script has Krishna make it in the hall. Confirm framing.
Duryodhana's 'needle's point' reply (suchyagram naiva dasyami, as commonly quoted) is paraphrased; confirm its location in the Udyoga Parva.
Krishna showing his cosmic form in the Kaurava court: stated as 'in the tradition'; confirm it is in the Udyoga Parva.
'Would have saved millions, in the story's numbers' refers to the eighteen akshauhinis; confirm the phrasing is acceptable.
